entries.meaning: Accident has 2 distinct senses.
examples: There was an accident on the highway this morning.
Most home accidents happen in the kitchen.
He broke his wrist in a bike accident.
There was an accident on the interstate this morning.
Most accidents happen within a few miles of home.
Nobody was hurt in the accident.

senses.head: Something bad that happens by chance and hurts someone or damages something
examples: There was an accident on the highway this morning.
Most home accidents happen in the kitchen.
He broke his wrist in a bike accident.

senses.head: A crash in which vehicles or people are hurt or damaged
examples: There was an accident on the interstate this morning.
Most accidents happen within a few miles of home.
Nobody was hurt in the accident.

entries.meaning: A door kept clear so people can leave a building or vehicle quickly in danger. ---
examples: The emergency exit is at the back of the store.
Please locate the two nearest emergency exits.
Never block an emergency exit with boxes.

entries.meaning: A device or signal that warns everyone in a building that there is a fire. ---
examples: Somebody pulled the fire alarm during third period.
The fire alarm went off at two in the morning.
All the fire alarms are tested twice a year.

entries.meaning: A metal cylinder of chemicals or foam used to put out a small fire. ---
examples: Keep a fire extinguisher under the kitchen sink.
He grabbed the fire extinguisher and aimed it at the base of the flames.
The fire extinguishers in the hallway were all expired.

entries.meaning: A small ceiling device that senses smoke and sounds a loud warning. ---
examples: The smoke detector goes off every time I make toast.
Change the battery in your smoke detector twice a year.
The landlord installed smoke detectors in every bedroom.

entries.meaning: A device that makes a loud sound when it senses smoke in a room. ---
examples: Our smoke alarm started chirping at midnight.
A working smoke alarm doubles your chance of getting out alive.
The fire department gives away free smoke alarms.
entries.contrast: Americans use smoke alarm and smoke detector for the same ceiling unit.

entries.meaning: A practice in which everyone leaves a building as if there were a fire. ---
examples: We had a fire drill right before lunch.
The school runs a fire drill every month.
Nobody takes fire drills seriously until there's a real fire.

entries.meaning: A lighted sign that shows the way out of a building. ---
examples: Follow the green exit sign down the stairs.
The exit sign over the door was burned out.
Exit signs have to stay lit even in a power failure.
entries.contrast: Exit is said either /ˈɛɡzɪt/ or /ˈɛksɪt/ — both are normal American.

entries.meaning: Escape has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Their escape from the burning building was captured on video.
It was a narrow escape — the roof fell in a minute later.
Both escapes happened through a basement window.
For her, gardening is an escape.
Movies were his only escape that winter.
Cheap paperbacks offer a quick escape on a long flight.

senses.head: The act of getting away from a dangerous place or situation
examples: Their escape from the burning building was captured on video.
It was a narrow escape — the roof fell in a minute later.
Both escapes happened through a basement window.

senses.head: Something that lets you forget your troubles for a while
examples: For her, gardening is an escape.
Movies were his only escape that winter.
Cheap paperbacks offer a quick escape on a long flight.

entries.русский: спасение бегством, побег; отдушина, способ отвлечься

entries.meaning: The path people are meant to follow to get out of danger. ---
examples: Plan an escape route from every room in the house.
The smoke cut off their only escape route.
Escape routes are marked on the back of the hotel door.

entries.meaning: An act of saving someone from danger. ---
examples: The rescue took six hours in freezing water.
Divers came to the rescue of the trapped crew.
The crew has made more than forty rescues this year.

entries.meaning: A person who saves someone from danger. ---
examples: Her rescuer was a neighbor with a ladder.
Rescuers dug through the snow for two days.
The rescuers reached the hikers just before dark.

entries.meaning: A police officer, firefighter, or medical worker who is first to arrive at an emergency. ---
examples: The first responder on the scene was a volunteer firefighter.
First responders pulled two people from the car.
The town held a breakfast to thank its first responders.

entries.meaning: The part of a hospital that treats people who need help immediately. ---
examples: We spent five hours in the emergency room.
Take him to the emergency room if the bleeding doesn't stop.
Rural emergency rooms are closing all over the state.
entries.contrast: Americans shorten this to the ER; the British say A&E.

entries.meaning: Warning has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The storm hit without any warning.
He ignored the warnings and swam out anyway.
The weather service issued a warning for three counties.
The officer let me off with a warning.
He got a written warning from his manager.
One more warning and you're off the team.

senses.head: Something said or shown to tell people that danger is coming
examples: The storm hit without any warning.
He ignored the warnings and swam out anyway.
The weather service issued a warning for three counties.

senses.head: An official caution given instead of a punishment, telling someone not to do it again
examples: The officer let me off with a warning.
He got a written warning from his manager.
One more warning and you're off the team.

entries.meaning: A sign that tells people about a danger ahead. ---
examples: A yellow warning sign marks the drop-off.
Somebody had knocked over the warning sign.
Warning signs were posted all along the fence.

entries.meaning: Printed text on a product that tells you how it can hurt you. ---
examples: Read the warning label before you use the cleaner.
The bottle carries a warning label about fumes.
Warning labels on ladders are there for a reason.

entries.meaning: Care taken to avoid danger or mistakes. ---
examples: Handle the gas can with caution.
Drivers should use extra caution on wet roads.
A little caution would have prevented the whole thing.

entries.meaning: Something you do in advance to keep harm from happening. ---
examples: Wearing a helmet is a simple precaution.
They took every precaution before the storm.
The usual precautions weren't enough this time.

entries.meaning: The state of being kept safe from harm, or the means of keeping something safe. ---
examples: These gloves offer good protection against cuts.
The wall gave them protection from the wind.
Sunscreen is your best protection on the water.

entries.meaning: The work of stopping something bad before it happens. ---
examples: The talk was about fire prevention in older homes.
Prevention is cheaper than a rescue.
Accident prevention is part of every shift meeting.

entries.meaning: Survivor has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The only survivor was a boy in the back seat.
Crews searched the rubble for survivors.
Survivors were taken to a shelter downtown.
Don't worry about her — she's a survivor.
He lost the business twice and started over at fifty; the man is a real survivor.
After the year she's had, I'd call her a survivor.

senses.head: A person who stays alive through an accident or disaster
examples: The only survivor was a boy in the back seat.
Crews searched the rubble for survivors.
Survivors were taken to a shelter downtown.

senses.head: Someone who keeps going and copes well no matter what happens to them
examples: Don't worry about her — she's a survivor.
He lost the business twice and started over at fifty; the man is a real survivor.
After the year she's had, I'd call her a survivor.

entries.русский: выживший, уцелевший; живучий человек, тот, кто не сдаётся

entries.meaning: Disaster has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The flood was the worst disaster in the county's history.
Natural disasters cost the state billions last year.
The governor declared the fire a disaster.
The dinner party was a disaster from start to finish.
His first attempt at cutting my hair was a disaster.
The movie was a box-office disaster.

senses.head: A sudden event that causes great damage or loss of life
examples: The flood was the worst disaster in the county's history.
Natural disasters cost the state billions last year.
The governor declared the fire a disaster.

senses.head: A complete failure, or something that has gone badly wrong
examples: The dinner party was a disaster from start to finish.
His first attempt at cutting my hair was a disaster.
The movie was a box-office disaster.

entries.meaning: A disaster of the very worst kind. ---
examples: A leak that size could turn into a catastrophe.
The dam failure was an avoidable catastrophe.
Two catastrophes in one summer emptied the relief fund.
entries.contrast: The final -e is pronounced: kuh-TAS-truh-fee, with the stress on the second syllable.

entries.meaning: Collision has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The collision happened at the intersection.
Nobody was hurt in the collision.
Head-on collisions are the deadliest kind.
The hearing exposed a collision between science and politics.
The movie is about the collision of two very different cultures.
Their ambitions put the two men on a collision course.

senses.head: A crash in which two moving things hit each other
examples: The collision happened at the intersection.
Nobody was hurt in the collision.
Head-on collisions are the deadliest kind.

senses.head: A sharp clash between opposing ideas, groups, or interests
examples: The hearing exposed a collision between science and politics.
The movie is about the collision of two very different cultures.
Their ambitions put the two men on a collision course.

entries.meaning: An event, usually an unpleasant one, that has to be reported or dealt with. ---
examples: The incident was over before the police arrived.
File a report after any incident on the job site.
There have been three incidents at that crossing this year.

entries.meaning: A small accident that causes trouble but little harm. ---
examples: We got there after a couple of mishaps with the trailer.
A kitchen mishap set off the smoke alarm.

entries.meaning: A crash in which many vehicles run into one another. ---
examples: Fog caused a twenty-car pileup on the interstate.
The pileup closed both lanes until evening.
Winter pileups are common on that stretch.
entries.contrast: One word as a noun (a pileup), two as a verb (cars piled up).

entries.meaning: A minor car crash that damages the body of the car but hurts nobody. ---
examples: It was just a fender bender in the parking lot.
Her first fender bender raised the insurance rate.
Two fender benders on the same corner in one week.
entries.contrast: American and informal; the British would say a bump or a prang.

entries.meaning: The place where a plane, train, or vehicle came down or wrecked. ---
examples: Investigators spent a week at the crash site.
The crash site is still closed to the public.

entries.meaning: A landing a pilot has to make right away because something has gone wrong. ---
examples: The plane made an emergency landing in a cornfield.
Smoke in the cabin forced an emergency landing.
The airport handles a few emergency landings a year.

entries.meaning: Collapse has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The collapse trapped four workers in the basement.
Heavy snow caused the roof collapse.

The collapse of the bank wiped out their savings.
Nobody at the firm predicted the collapse of the housing market.
The talks ended in collapse after three days.

senses.head: The sudden falling down of a building, roof, or other structure
examples: The collapse trapped four workers in the basement.
Heavy snow caused the roof collapse.
Two collapses in one week shut down the mine.

senses.head: A sudden and complete failure of a system, business, or plan
examples: The collapse of the bank wiped out their savings.
Nobody at the firm predicted the collapse of the housing market.
The talks ended in collapse after three days.

entries.meaning: Blast has 3 distinct senses.
examples: The blast blew out windows two blocks away.

Neighbors heard two blasts before the fire started.
We had a blast at the lake.
The party was a blast.
Her birthday trip was an absolute blast.
A blast from the ship's horn made us jump.
Three short blasts of the whistle meant trouble.
The band opened with a blast of trumpets.

senses.head: A violent explosion, or the rush of air it sends out
examples: The blast blew out windows two blocks away.
She was knocked down by the blast.
Neighbors heard two blasts before the fire started.

senses.head: A very enjoyable time
examples: We had a blast at the lake.
The party was a blast.
Her birthday trip was an absolute blast.

senses.head: A sudden loud sound from a horn, whistle, or instrument
examples: A blast from the ship's horn made us jump.
Three short blasts of the whistle meant trouble.
The band opened with a blast of trumpets.

entries.meaning: What is left of a vehicle or building that has been destroyed. ---

entries.meaning: Very great damage over a wide area. ---
examples: The devastation along the coast was hard to look at.

entries.meaning: A death caused by an accident, disaster, or violence. ---
examples: There was one fatality in the crash.
The fire caused no fatalities.

entries.meaning: The number of people killed by a disaster or accident. ---
examples: The death toll rose to nineteen overnight.
Officials expect the death toll to climb.

entries.meaning: A person who has been moved away from a dangerous area. ---

entries.meaning: An official instruction telling people they must leave an area. ---

entries.meaning: A period when people must stay inside a building or area for safety. ---

Two lockdowns in one semester rattled the parents.
entries.contrast: One word as a noun (a lockdown), two as a verb (they lock down the building).

entries.meaning: Refuge has 2 distinct senses.
examples: They took refuge in the basement.
The church offered refuge to families who lost their homes.
Hikers found refuge from the storm in an old cabin.
The lake is part of a national wildlife refuge.
Thousands of birds winter in the refuge.

senses.head: Shelter or safety from danger or bad weather
examples: They took refuge in the basement.
The church offered refuge to families who lost their homes.
Hikers found refuge from the storm in an old cabin.

senses.head: A place that gives protection, especially an area set aside for wild animals
examples: The lake is part of a national wildlife refuge.
Thousands of birds winter in the refuge.
She spent a month in a refuge for women leaving violent homes.

entries.meaning: A strong underground or reinforced room where people wait out a tornado or hurricane. ---

senses.head: A later effect or reaction that follows a shocking event

senses.head: A small shaking of the ground

senses.head: A slight uncontrollable shaking of the body or voice
examples: There was a tremor in her voice as she read the letter.

senses.head: Gas escaping from a pipe or fitting where it should not

senses.head: Something that takes away a bad feeling or improves a bad situation

examples: Somebody knocked over a traffic cone.

The crew set out a traffic cone every twenty feet.

entries.meaning: Bright yellow plastic ribbon strung around a dangerous or restricted area. ---
examples: They ran caution tape across the driveway.
Don't step past the caution tape.
There was caution tape around the whole block.

entries.meaning: Roadblock has 2 distinct senses.
examples: There's a roadblock at the bottom of the hill.
Police set up a roadblock on the bridge.
Roadblocks kept everyone out of the burn area.
Funding turned out to be the biggest roadblock.
We hit a roadblock when the supplier backed out.
Their lawyers threw up one roadblock after another.

senses.head: A barrier across a road that stops or turns back traffic
examples: There's a roadblock at the bottom of the hill.
Police set up a roadblock on the bridge.
Roadblocks kept everyone out of the burn area.

senses.head: Something that stops progress on a plan or project
examples: Funding turned out to be the biggest roadblock.
We hit a roadblock when the supplier backed out.
Their lawyers threw up one roadblock after another.

entries.meaning: A raised strip across a road that forces drivers to slow down. ---
examples: Take the speed bump slowly or you'll scrape the bumper.
The school asked the city for a speed bump.
There are four speed bumps in the parking lot.

entries.meaning: Emergency brake has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Set the emergency brake on that hill.
The emergency brake was frozen solid.
Emergency brakes rust if you never use them.
Someone pulled the emergency brake between stations.
There is an emergency brake at each end of the car.
Misusing the emergency brake carries a heavy fine.

senses.head: The separate brake that holds a parked car or stops it if the main brakes fail
examples: Set the emergency brake on that hill.
The emergency brake was frozen solid.
Emergency brakes rust if you never use them.

senses.head: A handle or valve that stops the train at once in a crisis
examples: Someone pulled the emergency brake between stations.
There is an emergency brake at each end of the car.
Misusing the emergency brake carries a heavy fine.

entries.contrast: Brake sounds exactly like break; the British call this the handbrake.

entries.meaning: Respirator has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Wear a respirator when you sand that paint.
His respirator fogged up in the heat.
The shop keeps respirators by the door.
He spent two weeks on a respirator after the accident.
The hospital ran short of respirators during the surge.
Doctors took her off the respirator on Sunday.

senses.head: A mask with filters that keeps dust, fumes, or germs out of the lungs
examples: Wear a respirator when you sand that paint.
His respirator fogged up in the heat.
The shop keeps respirators by the door.

senses.head: A machine that breathes for a patient who cannot breathe alone
examples: He spent two weeks on a respirator after the accident.
The hospital ran short of respirators during the surge.
Doctors took her off the respirator on Sunday.

entries.meaning: A light paper mask that keeps dust out of your nose and mouth. ---
examples: Grab a dust mask before you go in the attic.
A dust mask won't protect you from fumes.
Dust masks come ten to a box.

entries.meaning: A mask covering the whole face that filters out poisonous gas. ---
examples: The crew went in wearing gas masks.
His gas mask was fitted the week before.
A gas mask is useless without the right filter.

entries.meaning: A clear plastic guard worn over the whole face. ---
examples: Put a face shield on before you start grinding.
The face shield took the spark instead of his eye.
Face shields hang next to the goggles.

entries.meaning: Tough clear glasses worn to keep chips and dust out of the eyes. ---
examples: You need safety glasses to run that saw.
My safety glasses are scratched up.
The shop hands out three pairs of safety glasses a year.
entries.contrast: Plural only — count them in pairs: a pair of safety glasses.

entries.meaning: A bright orange or yellow vest that makes a worker easy to see. ---
examples: Everybody on the site wears a safety vest.
Her safety vest was hanging on the truck mirror.
The crossing guards got new safety vests.

entries.meaning: The clothing and equipment worn to keep a worker from being hurt. ---
examples: Firefighters carry sixty pounds of protective gear.
All of the protective gear is stored in that locker.
You can't enter the lab without protective gear.
entries.contrast: Uncountable in English: a lot of protective gear, never a protective gear.

entries.meaning: A sealed full-body suit worn around dangerous chemicals or germs. ---
examples: Two workers in hazmat suits went into the tank room.
The hazmat suit gets unbearably hot in ten minutes.
They keep four hazmat suits on the truck.
entries.contrast: Hazmat is short for hazardous materials.

entries.meaning: An inflatable boat carried on a ship or plane for use if it sinks or ditches. ---
examples: The crew climbed into the life raft.
The life raft inflates as soon as it hits the water.
Both life rafts were found empty.

entries.meaning: A ring or vest that keeps a person floating in the water. ---
examples: He threw her a life preserver from the dock.
There's a life preserver on each side of the boat.
The life preservers were locked in a cabinet.
entries.contrast: American; the British say lifebelt or lifebuoy.

entries.meaning: Anything designed to keep a person afloat in water. ---
examples: Your seat cushion can be used as a flotation device.
Children must wear a flotation device on the dock.
The store sells flotation devices for toddlers.

entries.meaning: Lifeline has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The loan was a lifeline for the family business.
The ferry is the island's only lifeline in winter.
For a lot of seniors, that daily call is a lifeline.
He tied a lifeline around his waist before going out on the ice.
A lifeline runs the length of the deck.
The radio was their only lifeline.

senses.head: Something that provides essential help or keeps something going
examples: The loan was a lifeline for the family business.
The ferry is the island's only lifeline in winter.
For a lot of seniors, that daily call is a lifeline.

senses.head: A rope thrown or fixed to keep someone from being lost or swept away
examples: He tied a lifeline around his waist before going out on the ice.
A lifeline runs the length of the deck.
The radio was their only lifeline.

entries.русский: спасательный круг, жизненно важная поддержка; страховочный трос, спасательный конец

entries.meaning: Distress has 2 distinct senses.
examples: She sued the company for emotional distress.
The fireworks caused the dogs obvious distress.
He hid his distress well, but his hands were shaking.
The boat was in distress about two miles out.
They picked up a distress call at midnight.
The plane signaled distress and turned back.

senses.head: Great mental pain, worry, or sorrow
examples: She sued the company for emotional distress.
The fireworks caused the dogs obvious distress.
He hid his distress well, but his hands were shaking.

senses.head: The state of being in serious trouble and needing help
examples: The boat was in distress about two miles out.
They picked up a distress call at midnight.
The plane signaled distress and turned back.

entries.русский: страдание, душевная боль; бедствие, тяжёлое положение

entries.meaning: The spoken radio call used by a ship or aircraft in serious danger. ---
examples: The pilot put out a mayday over the water.
The tower recorded the mayday at 4:12.
Two maydays came in during the storm.
entries.contrast: From French m'aidez ("help me") — nothing to do with the holiday May Day.

entries.meaning: A wide-barreled pistol that fires a signal flare into the sky. ---
examples: The boat carries a flare gun and three shells.
She fired the flare gun straight up.
Flare guns are checked with the rest of the safety kit.

entries.meaning: Beacon has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The plane's emergency beacon led searchers to the wreck.
A beacon flashes on top of the tower.
Climbers carry avalanche beacons.
The clinic became a beacon of hope for the whole valley.
Her third-grade teacher was a beacon in a hard year.
The paper was long seen as a beacon of free speech.

senses.head: A light or radio signal that guides rescuers or warns of danger
examples: The plane's emergency beacon led searchers to the wreck.
A beacon flashes on top of the tower.
Climbers carry avalanche beacons.

senses.head: A person or thing that gives other people hope or guidance
examples: The clinic became a beacon of hope for the whole valley.
Her third-grade teacher was a beacon in a hard year.
The paper was long seen as a beacon of free speech.

entries.meaning: A powerful lamp whose beam can be aimed to look for something in the dark. ---
examples: The helicopter's searchlight swept the field.
A searchlight found the boat near the rocks.
Two searchlights lit up the riverbank.

entries.meaning: A cone-shaped device that makes a voice loud enough for a crowd to hear. ---
examples: An officer gave directions through a megaphone.
The megaphone batteries died halfway through.
They handed out megaphones to the block captains.

entries.meaning: An electric megaphone used to shout instructions to a crowd. ---
examples: The fire chief shouted through a bullhorn.
Someone raised a bullhorn and told everyone to move back.
The police brought two bullhorns.
entries.contrast: American for megaphone; the British stick with megaphone or loudhailer.

entries.meaning: A small two-way radio you carry in your hand. ---
examples: Keep the walkie-talkie on channel three.
His walkie-talkie crackled and went dead.
The crew works with walkie-talkies inside the building.

entries.meaning: A phone line set up so people can get help or report a problem quickly. ---
examples: The county set up a hotline for storm damage.
She called the poison hotline at two in the morning.
Both hotlines were busy all night.

entries.meaning: A button pressed to call for help immediately. ---
examples: The teller hit the panic button under the counter.
Every room has a panic button by the bed.
The new alarm came with two panic buttons.

entries.meaning: A warning of danger that turns out to be wrong. ---
examples: It was only a false alarm — burned popcorn.
The department answers hundreds of false alarms a year.
After the third false alarm, nobody moved.

entries.meaning: The person a school or employer calls if something happens to you. ---
examples: Put your sister down as your emergency contact.
They couldn't reach his emergency contact.
The form asks for two emergency contacts.

entries.meaning: A packed set of supplies for staying alive until help arrives. ---
examples: Keep a survival kit in the car during winter.
The survival kit has water, a blanket, and matches.
They sell survival kits at the hardware store.

entries.meaning: A person paid to watch a building or area and keep it safe. ---
examples: The security guard walked us to our car.
A security guard found the broken window.
Two security guards work the night shift.

entries.meaning: A camera that records what happens in a building or on a street. ---
examples: A security camera caught the whole thing.
The security camera over the door isn't working.
There are security cameras in every hallway.

entries.meaning: A light that comes on to show something is wrong or dangerous. ---
examples: A red warning light came on over the door.
Don't ignore that warning light on the dash.
All the warning lights flashed at once.

entries.meaning: The rules and habits that keep fires from starting or spreading. ---
examples: The class covers fire safety in the home.
Fire safety starts with a clear exit path.
He teaches fire safety at the elementary school.

entries.meaning: The work of putting out fires. ---
examples: Firefighting is harder than it looks on television.
He spent thirty years in firefighting.
The town spends most of its budget on firefighting.

entries.meaning: A truck carrying a pump, hoses, and water to a fire. ---
examples: Three fire engines pulled up outside.
The fire engine couldn't get down the narrow street.
Kids waved at the fire engine in the parade.
entries.contrast: Americans say both fire engine and fire truck for the same vehicle.

entries.meaning: The building where firefighters and their trucks are based. ---
examples: The firehouse on Third Street has been there a century.
They hold a pancake breakfast at the firehouse.
Both firehouses closed in the budget cuts.
entries.contrast: A homey American word for fire station.

entries.meaning: A man whose job is putting out fires. ---
examples: A fireman carried the cat down the ladder.
Two firemen stayed behind to watch the embers.
My grandfather was a fireman for twenty years.
entries.contrast: Irregular plural firemen; the neutral modern word is firefighter.

entries.meaning: The officer in charge of a fire department. ---
examples: The fire chief spoke to reporters at the scene.
Our fire chief has been on the job since 1998.
Two former fire chiefs came to the ceremony.

entries.meaning: An official who inspects buildings and investigates the causes of fires. ---
examples: The fire marshal closed the club for overcrowding.
A fire marshal is still looking into the cause.
Fire marshals check every school in the county.
entries.contrast: Marshal sounds just like martial, and American spelling keeps only one l.

entries.meaning: The heavy hose that carries water from a hydrant or truck to a fire. ---
examples: It takes two people to hold a fire hose.
The fire hose was still charged with water.
Fire hoses ran across the whole intersection.

entries.meaning: A heavy door that holds back flames and smoke for a set time. ---
examples: Never prop open a fire door.
The fire door kept the smoke out of the stairwell.
All the fire doors close automatically when the alarm sounds.

entries.meaning: A sheet of fireproof cloth thrown over flames to smother them. ---
examples: She smothered the grease fire with a fire blanket.
A fire blanket hangs by the stove.
The lab keeps fire blankets at both exits.

entries.meaning: A folding ladder kept upstairs to climb out a window in a fire. ---
examples: There's an escape ladder under the bed.
The escape ladder hooks over the window sill.
We bought escape ladders for both bedrooms.

entries.meaning: A large, bright fire. ---
examples: Crews fought the blaze for six hours.
The blaze started in a back room.
Two blazes broke out the same night.

entries.meaning: A huge fire that is out of control. ---
examples: The warehouse became an inferno in minutes.
Firefighters could only watch the inferno from the street.
Summer infernos like this used to be rare.

entries.meaning: A person who sets fire to property on purpose.
examples: Investigators think an arsonist started it.
The arsonist used gasoline and a rag.
Two arsonists were arrested that fall.
